lessons.title: A line with intention
lessons.subtitle: Let your eye lead your hand.
lessons.idea: A useful line begins before the pencil touches the page. Choose a starting point and an ending point, rehearse the movement above the surface, then make one unhurried stroke. A slightly uneven line can still be confident.
lessons.observation: The dots in the study are destinations. Notice how each line travels between them without a cluster of little corrections. Confidence comes from committing to a direction, not from drawing perfectly straight.
steps: Connect each pair of dots with one stroke. Move from your arm as well as your fingers.
Switch to Faint and repeat beside the first lines. Try a different direction each time.
Choose Freehand. Draw five new pairs of dots and connect them without tracing.
lessons.check: Can I see a clear beginning and end in each stroke?
lessons.transfer: Draw the long edges of a book in front of you, using one stroke for each edge.

workshop.setup: Use a pencil or the Pencil tool. Give your arm room to move; keep the page or device steady and use a comfortable, light pressure.
workshop.demonstration: Start by choosing two destinations rather than thinking about a finished line. Move your hand above the page along the route twice, noticing which movement feels easiest. Lower the tip and make one stroke at a pace that you can sustain. Then lift it and look. Compare the stroke with your intention: did it leave the first point clearly, travel in one direction, and stop near the destination? Make the next attempt beside it rather than repeatedly repairing the first. Rotate the paper when a direction feels awkward. On a fixed device, change your arm position instead of forcing your wrist into an extreme bend. As confidence improves, vary the length and slope while keeping the same sequence of look, rehearse, commit, and review. This exercise trains a repeatable decision, not a talent for perfectly straight marks.
workshop.mistakes: A fuzzy bundle of tiny corrections usually means you are judging the line while still drawing it. Pause, rehearse the complete movement, and try once more in a new place. If strokes overshoot, slow down before the endpoint. Pressing harder cannot compensate for an uncertain direction and makes corrections more conspicuous.
workshop.challenge: Make a page of twelve strokes: four short, four medium, and four long. Include a horizontal, vertical, and diagonal direction in each group. Circle the most deliberate stroke in each group and describe its start and finish. Finally draw a nearby book with one line per long edge; accept small deviations without retracing them.

lessons.title: Curves that breathe
lessons.subtitle: Build rhythm with C and S curves.
lessons.idea: Curves carry movement. A C curve bends in one direction; an S curve changes direction around an inflection point. Think about the whole gesture rather than slowly assembling a curve from short pieces.
lessons.observation: Follow the outer sweep of the examples. The widest bend sits away from the endpoints. In the S curve, the change of direction is gradual rather than a sharp corner.
steps: Trace the three curves once, following their full movement.
With a faint guide, draw a second curve just inside each original.
Hide the guide and invent a leaf, a ribbon, and a wave using only C and S curves.
lessons.check: Do my curves change direction smoothly?
lessons.transfer: Find three curves in a houseplant and draw their movement without the small details.

workshop.setup: Keep the reference visible beside your drawing for the first pass. Start with the Pencil tool and leave enough space to draw each curve again.
workshop.demonstration: Follow a ribbon's full movement with your eyes before drawing its edges. A C curve keeps turning in one direction, while an S curve passes through a gradual change of direction. Place the two endpoints and imagine the widest part of the bend. Rehearse that broad route, then draw it without trying to describe the ribbon's thickness. Add a second line beside the first and compare whether it preserves the same rhythm. Where the ribbon turns, the visible edge may narrow or overlap; those details belong after the main movement is established. Repeat the gesture more slowly, then at a slightly quicker pace. Neither speed is automatically better: choose the one that keeps the motion continuous and lets you arrive at the endpoint deliberately. In the independent pass, invent a new curve with the same kind of movement rather than reproducing the exact source.
workshop.mistakes: A sharp corner at the middle of an S often comes from thinking of it as two separate C shapes. Rehearse the entire change of direction in one movement. If every curve looks cramped, move from the elbow and shoulder as well as the fingers. Avoid adding thickness until the gesture itself feels convincing.
workshop.challenge: Draw three C curves with different depths, then three S curves with different locations for their change of direction. Turn two into ribbons by adding a second boundary. Make a final small drawing of a wave, leaf, or loose cord using the same movements. Compare which curves feel relaxed and which still hesitate.

lessons.title: The ellipse warm-up
lessons.subtitle: Give circles a sense of space.
lessons.idea: An ellipse describes a circle seen at an angle. Its two halves mirror around a long axis and a short axis. As a circular opening tilts away from you, it appears flatter, but the ends remain rounded.
lessons.observation: The center lines divide each ellipse into balanced halves. Compare the narrow opening with the rounder one. Avoid turning the ends into points: an ellipse is not an almond shape.
steps: Rehearse each oval in the air, then draw around it in one movement.
Use Faint and add the long and short axes before drawing each ellipse.
Without a guide, draw five ellipses from nearly flat to nearly circular.
lessons.check: Are both ends rounded and both halves balanced?
lessons.transfer: Look down into a cup, then lower your eye level and sketch how its opening changes.

workshop.setup: Use a light pencil and keep construction marks visible. The bowl reference is an observation target; the simple diagram is a guide to the axes.
workshop.demonstration: First find the opening's longest visible direction and draw a light center axis along it. Mark the midpoint and place the shorter axis across it. Use those four endpoints to rehearse the entire ellipse above the page. When you draw, let the ends remain rounded; there is no sharp change of direction at the side points. Check the two halves on either side of each axis. They need to feel balanced even when the ellipse is narrow. Then compare the inner rim with the outer boundary. The visible strip between them describes the bowl's thickness, so keep those curves related. Do not assume that the lower edge of the bowl is another identical oval: it is a separate visible contour. For the final pass, imagine raising or lowering your viewpoint and predict how the opening would become more or less open.
workshop.mistakes: Pointed ends make an ellipse resemble an almond. Slow down around the side turns without stopping there. A lopsided ellipse often comes from placing the short axis away from the midpoint. Check the center before redrawing. Avoid going around the same oval many times in the hope that one of the lines will become correct.
workshop.challenge: Draw a sequence of five ellipses from a narrow opening to an almost circular view, all with the same long-axis length. Add the axes and choose two to develop into simple bowls. If you have a real cup, change your eye level and compare the prediction with what you actually see.

lessons.title: Weight tells a story
lessons.subtitle: Make some edges speak louder.
lessons.idea: Line weight creates hierarchy. A heavier edge can suggest overlap, a shadow, or a focal point. Lighter marks can describe a lit edge or an early construction. Weight works best when it has a reason.
lessons.observation: The overlapping shapes use stronger lines where one form passes in front of another. The light construction lines remain visible, but they do not compete with the main edges.
steps: Draw all three forms lightly with the pencil tool.
Choose Ink and strengthen only the edges that overlap another form.
Hide the guide and draw three new overlapping objects. Leave the distant edges light.
lessons.check: Can I tell which form is in front without adding shading?
lessons.transfer: Sketch a folded cloth and strengthen just the edges where one fold covers another.

workshop.setup: Begin with the Pencil tool for construction and use Ink only for selected final edges. Keep the shapes large enough to compare their overlaps.
workshop.demonstration: Draw the main solids with the same light pressure at first. Identify the nearest object and follow its contour to a place where it hides another object. Strengthen that continuous front edge; allow the interrupted rear edge to stop. Next choose one boundary in light that can remain lighter. Compare the result before adding any other emphasis. The goal is a hierarchy, so a small number of stronger marks should organize the whole group. Weight may also describe a shadowed lower edge, but it should still have a reason. Step back or reduce the drawing on screen: if every boundary attracts equal attention, the hierarchy has disappeared. In the final pass, remove one heavy edge or leave a quiet section open and check whether the spatial order remains clear. A convincing arrangement often needs fewer strong marks than you expect.
workshop.mistakes: A thick outline around every shape makes them look like flat stickers. Decide where one object actually passes in front of another before strengthening the line. Do not use heavy ink to hide an incorrect proportion; check the light construction first. If one dark corner dominates accidentally, balance it through deliberate simplification elsewhere rather than thickening everything.
workshop.challenge: Draw three overlapping household forms twice. In the first version, keep all contours equally light. In the second, emphasize only four short overlap or shadow edges. Compare the versions at thumbnail size and describe which depth relationships became clearer. Make one final version using only the minimum dark marks you need.

lessons.title: One continuous contour
lessons.subtitle: Slow down and follow an edge.
lessons.idea: Contour drawing trains attention. Your eye follows an object's boundary while your hand records the journey. Resist naming the parts: look instead for changes in direction, tight bends, and long stretches.
lessons.observation: The leaf's outline changes pace: it widens, narrows, and returns to the stem. The central vein is a separate decision. A contour can describe an object with very few marks.
steps: Follow the leaf outline slowly without lifting your pencil.
Repeat with a faint guide, paying attention to where the edge changes direction.
Hide the guide and draw a nearby leaf or spoon in one continuous line.
lessons.check: Did I follow what I saw rather than a symbol for the object?
lessons.transfer: Spend two minutes drawing your free hand while looking mostly at the hand.

workshop.setup: Choose a comfortable line width and give the whole leaf room on the page. Spend a few moments looking at the stem and outer boundary before starting.
workshop.demonstration: Pick a point near the leaf's stem and follow the boundary with your eyes. Notice the long broad sweep, the tighter turns, and the shallow notch. Now let your hand follow that same journey in one continuous line. Slow down where the edge changes direction, but avoid stopping to repair every small deviation. The drawing may wander; the important question is whether you kept observing the actual sequence of turns. After the first pass, compare the leaf's widest point and its total width-to-height relationship. Make a second contour beside it, correcting one large relationship while preserving the continuous attention. Add the stem or central vein only after the outside shape reads. For the independent pass, look at a real object for longer than you look at your page. This changes the exercise from copying a symbol into recording observation.
workshop.mistakes: A symmetrical generic leaf often means you have drawn what you know instead of following the source. Name a specific irregularity before the next pass. If the drawing becomes a series of disconnected scratches, choose a larger scale and follow a longer stretch at a time. Resist filling the interior with veins to compensate for an uncertain contour.
workshop.challenge: Make three two-minute contours: one from the reference, one from your free hand, and one from a spoon or leaf nearby. Keep the pencil down as much as practical. Compare the speed of your eye with the speed of your hand, then write one sentence about a turn you noticed only after slowing down.

lessons.title: Big shapes first
lessons.subtitle: Find the simple structure beneath detail.
lessons.idea: Complex subjects become manageable when you begin with large shapes. An envelope is a simple outer boundary that contains the subject. Place that boundary before describing any small indentation or feature.
lessons.observation: The pear fits inside a broad envelope. Its upper mass is smaller than its lower mass. Those relationships make it recognizable before you add the stem or refine the contour.
steps: Sketch the angular outer envelope with light strokes.
Place the two main masses inside it, then connect their edges.
Hide the guide and draw a different piece of fruit, beginning with its envelope.
lessons.check: Does the large shape read before I add details?
lessons.transfer: Reduce a shoe to three large shapes before drawing any laces.

workshop.setup: Use the reference at a comfortable viewing size. Begin with a light construction and postpone all surface texture and tiny features.
workshop.demonstration: Find the subject's highest, lowest, leftmost, and rightmost visible points. Join those landmarks with a few straight segments to create an envelope that could contain the whole pear. Compare its total width with its height before doing anything inside it. Then divide that envelope into the broad lower mass and the narrower upper mass. Their overlap gives you a simple structure to refine. Replace one straight segment at a time with an observed curve, checking how the boundary approaches the stem and base. Preserve useful construction marks rather than erasing them immediately; they show what you changed and why. When the pear reads clearly at a distance, add the stem as a directional accent. Surface spots belong last, and you may not need them at all. Repeat the block-in at a smaller scale to test whether the large relationships survived.
workshop.mistakes: A detailed stem cannot rescue a body that is too narrow. Return to the full envelope when the subject feels wrong. Avoid using many tiny segments in the first block-in: five or six clear directions are easier to compare. If both masses become perfect circles, check their actual asymmetry and the way they join.
workshop.challenge: Choose a shoe, fruit, or small bag and draw two envelopes for it without details. Develop the more convincing envelope into a contour drawing. Stop after ten minutes and view it from a distance. Write which large relationship made the object recognizable, then compare that relationship with the original object once more.

lessons.title: Drawing the spaces
lessons.subtitle: Look at what surrounds the subject.
lessons.idea: Negative space is the shape around or between objects. Drawing a gap can be easier than drawing a familiar object, because you have fewer assumptions about what that gap should look like.
lessons.observation: Study the opening inside the handle and the space beside the cup. These spaces have their own proportions. If the opening is too wide, the handle will feel wrong even when its outer edge is smooth.
steps: Draw the empty opening in the handle before drawing the cup.
Add the outside edges, keeping the opening intact.
With Freehand selected, draw the gaps between two fingers of your free hand.
lessons.check: Do the empty shapes have the right width and height?
lessons.transfer: Sketch a chair by drawing the spaces between its legs first.

workshop.setup: Keep the cup and its handle opening fully visible. Use a light line and reserve a separate space for your independent study.
workshop.demonstration: Begin inside the handle rather than on the cup's outer boundary. Compare the opening's height, width, and main tilt as if it were an unfamiliar flat shape. Draw that shape alone and check it against the source. Next build the handle's thickness around it, paying attention to where the thickness changes near its attachments. Place the cup body in relation to the opening rather than starting again with an unrelated outline. Compare the space beside the cup with the hole you have drawn. Both negative shapes can reveal a proportion error in the positive form. Add only enough overlap and shadow to explain how the handle joins the vessel. In a second study, begin with a different empty space, such as the gap between two fingers, to transfer the same way of looking to a subject with different associations.
workshop.mistakes: A handle often looks wrong because its opening is too wide, even when the outer curve is smooth. Correct the negative shape before refining the line quality. Do not assume the handle has uniform thickness. If the cup body drifts while you work on the handle, compare the distance from the opening to the far side of the cup.
workshop.challenge: Draw the handle opening, a chair-leg gap, and the space between two fingers as three isolated flat shapes. Then develop one into a complete object. Give the empty shapes as much attention as the object itself. Finish by identifying a proportion correction that became easier when you looked at the space instead.

lessons.title: Measure relationships
lessons.subtitle: Compare sizes instead of guessing.
lessons.idea: Proportion is a relationship, not an isolated measurement. Choose one length as a unit and compare everything else with it. Ask how many widths fit into a height, and where important landmarks fall.
lessons.observation: The bottle is divided into quarters. Its shoulder, neck, and base can be located by comparing them with the whole height. The horizontal marks help you check both sides together.
steps: Draw a center line and mark the top and bottom.
Divide the height into four equal parts and place the neck and shoulders.
Hide the guide and draw a real bottle, checking width against height.
lessons.check: Can I describe my object's height in units of its width?
lessons.transfer: Compare a mug and a bottle side by side using the mug's height as one unit.

workshop.setup: Pick one measuring unit and keep it consistent. You can use a pencil held at arm's length when observing a real object; on screen, compare visually against the reference.
workshop.demonstration: Place the bottle's top and bottom first. Compare the full height with its widest visible width, then choose one of those lengths as your unit. Locate the shoulder and neck by asking where they fall within that whole height. A quarter division can be a useful starting check, but the particular bottle may not match an exact quarter: observation takes priority. Draw a light center direction through the bottle and compare both sides at the same heights. Then inspect the spaces around it. These checks can reveal a lean or a shoulder that is wider on one side. Add the outer contour only after the landmarks agree. In the independent pass, draw a different bottle at a different size while preserving its measured relationships. Measuring is a way to structure looking, not a requirement to turn every drawing into a diagram.
workshop.mistakes: Measuring each small part in isolation can produce a collection of accurate fragments that do not fit together. Keep returning to the whole height and width. Do not let the centerline become a rule that forces a naturally irregular object into perfect symmetry. If the neck seems crooked, compare its direction before adding the lip.
workshop.challenge: Draw a real bottle with only five landmarks: top, bottom, widest left, widest right, and shoulder height. Build the outline around them, then add a nearby cup using the bottle's width as a shared unit. Explain one ratio in words and check it against the actual arrangement before finishing.

lessons.title: Angles before outlines
lessons.subtitle: Block in a subject with straight lines.
lessons.idea: A block-in uses a small number of straight segments to describe a complex silhouette. Straight segments make slopes easier to compare. Curves can come later, after the overall direction is convincing.
lessons.observation: The mountain contour can be reduced to a few slopes. Check each segment against an imaginary horizontal. A small angle error can shift the highest point much farther than you expect.
steps: Draw the angular mountain outline with five or six strokes.
Check where each peak sits relative to the valley beside it.
Hide the guide and block in the silhouette of a crumpled cloth using straight lines.
lessons.check: Have I compared the steepness of neighboring slopes?
lessons.transfer: Block in the outside shape of a plant without drawing individual leaves.

workshop.setup: Use a light, broad line and allow the entire silhouette to fit inside the page. Keep your attention on slopes rather than on the names of the forms.
workshop.demonstration: Treat the outside boundary as a sequence of straight directions. Mark the highest and lowest points, then choose five or six places where the silhouette changes direction most clearly. Compare each slope with an imagined horizontal or vertical. Draw the longest and most important segments first, and check how their endpoints align across the whole subject. A steepness error near the beginning can move a later landmark surprisingly far, so correct the structural relationship before adding curves. When the angular block-in feels convincing, soften only the segments that need to become curved. The straight version should still remain understandable beneath the refinement. For a second pass, use fewer segments than before and ask which turns are essential. This selective simplification is useful for landscapes, fabric, plants, and any complex subject with a readable outer shape.
workshop.mistakes: A busy zigzag is not necessarily a useful block-in. Too many small segments make the larger slopes difficult to compare. If a peak moves sideways, check the neighboring slopes rather than shifting the peak alone. Avoid using tiny curves to disguise a large angle error; return to the straight construction and make a clear correction.
workshop.challenge: Block in a crumpled cloth using six straight segments, then repeat using ten. Compare which version communicates the whole shape more clearly. Develop one version with a few curved refinements and leave the other angular. Finish by drawing a plant silhouette in the same way without describing individual leaves.

lessons.title: A grid you can leave behind
lessons.subtitle: Use structure, then trust your eye.
lessons.idea: A grid breaks a large problem into smaller comparisons. Look for where a contour crosses a cell edge. The purpose is to train observation, so eventually reduce the help and redraw without it.
lessons.observation: The leaf crosses several cells. Notice its widest point and where the stem meets a grid line. Compare crossings rather than copying each square as an isolated picture.
steps: Copy the leaf by locating its intersections with the grid.
Choose Faint and connect those landmarks with a continuous contour.
Choose Freehand and redraw the leaf beside your first study from memory.
lessons.check: Does my second drawing keep the same large proportions?
lessons.transfer: In the reference studio, use the grid on your own photo, then try the subject again on paper without it.

workshop.setup: Use the grid as a temporary measuring aid. Keep it faint enough that the leaf remains the subject, and plan room for a second drawing without the grid.
workshop.demonstration: Choose a few landmarks where the leaf crosses the grid rather than copying one cell at a time. Start with the stem base, topmost tip, widest point, and a distinctive notch. Compare each crossing with the midpoint or corner of its cell. Place those landmarks on your own grid, then connect them across several cells with a continuous contour. This keeps the object whole instead of turning it into separate little fragments. Check the large width-to-height relationship after the first contour. For the next pass, reduce the guide and rely more on the landmarks you have already understood. In the final pass, hide the grid and reconstruct the same subject from its main directions. Reveal the source only after completing that attempt, and choose one relationship to correct. The grid is successful when it makes the next independent drawing easier.
workshop.mistakes: A drawing can match individual squares and still feel fragmented. Compare the long contour across cell boundaries and redraw it as one movement. If grid lines dominate, lighten them or use fewer. Avoid treating the memory pass as a test you must pass perfectly; use the mismatch to decide what to observe next.
workshop.challenge: Make a grid-assisted study, a faintly guided study, and a small independent version of one leaf. Compare only three things: total proportion, widest point, and stem direction. Record which changed most when the grid disappeared. Repeat the method with a photo you own, using fewer landmarks than in the first attempt.

lessons.title: Five steps of value
lessons.subtitle: Describe light before adding color.
lessons.idea: Value means how light or dark something appears. A small set of clearly separated values can describe a subject more effectively than many uncertain shades. Keep your lightest paper area available for the brightest light.
lessons.observation: The five squares progress from paper white to dark ink. The middle steps should remain distinguishable. The challenge is separation, not a perfectly smooth transition.
steps: Leave the first square empty and fill the last with dense hatching.
Build three middle values by varying the spacing and layering of strokes.
Hide the guide and create another five-step scale without looking at the first.
lessons.check: Can I distinguish every neighboring pair when I squint?
lessons.transfer: Choose three values to describe a white object beside a window.

workshop.setup: Use one drawing tool for the whole exercise so changes in tone come mainly from your marks. Keep a patch of untouched paper available for the lightest value.
workshop.demonstration: Make five equal working areas, leaving the first as paper and building the last to your darkest comfortable tone. Fill the middle areas by changing stroke spacing and adding deliberate layers. Compare neighboring patches frequently: each pair should remain visibly different. The middle value is particularly useful because it helps you judge both lighter and darker areas. Step back or squint to simplify the comparison; a patch that looks complex up close may merge with its neighbor at a distance. Once the scale is clear, use three of its values to describe a simple object. Reserve the light family before adding the shadow family. The exercise is about choosing a small, readable set of values, not achieving a perfectly smooth finish. A textured patch can still have a very clear overall lightness.
workshop.mistakes: If the two middle patches look identical, change one decisively rather than adding uncertain marks to both. A dark outline around each patch can distort the comparison, so keep the boundaries light. Do not press excessively to make the darkest square; additional controlled layers are often more useful and easier to repeat.
workshop.challenge: Build one five-step scale with parallel hatching and another with crosshatching. Choose three values from either scale to draw a white object near a window. Compare the object study at a small size and check whether its broad light and shadow remain separate. Write which value you used too often and would simplify next time.

lessons.title: Light around a sphere
lessons.subtitle: Turn a flat circle into a solid form.
lessons.idea: A sphere turns gradually away from a light source. Separate the light family from the shadow family first, then add intermediate values. The cast shadow rests on the surface beneath the object and helps locate it in space.
lessons.observation: Light comes from the upper left. The lower right of the sphere belongs to shadow, and the cast shadow extends rightward. Preserve a light area rather than outlining a bright highlight.
steps: Draw the circular silhouette lightly and mark the direction of light.
Build the shadow side with curved hatching; keep the lit side open.
Hide the guide and draw another sphere lit from the opposite direction.
lessons.check: Do the sphere's shading and cast shadow agree on the light direction?
lessons.transfer: Place an egg near one lamp and identify the light and shadow families before drawing.

workshop.setup: Use a single reference light direction throughout the study. Begin with a light circle, and keep the page or device's pale background for your brightest light.
workshop.demonstration: Compare the sphere with the cylinder and cube in the reference, noticing that the sphere's surface turns gradually rather than breaking into flat planes. Draw its silhouette and mark the light direction beside the study. Locate the broad boundary between the light-facing and shadow-facing parts. Build a restrained shadow family first; do not blend everything into an even gray. Add intermediate hatching where the surface turns, leaving the lit area quieter. The cast shadow is a separate shape on the table, and its contact with the sphere helps ground the form. Compare the darkest contact area with the softer outer shadow edge. Any reflected light within the shadow should remain subordinate to the main light family in this setup. In a second pass, change the imagined light direction and make the shading and cast shadow change together.
workshop.mistakes: A dark ring around the silhouette can flatten the sphere. Let the interior values do more of the work. If the cast shadow points toward the light, stop and compare the whole lighting setup. Avoid turning reflected light into a bright stripe; check its value against the actual lit surface before emphasizing it.
workshop.challenge: Draw two spheres at the same size, one from the reference and one lit from the opposite side. Use three values in the first and five in the second. Compare whether the extra values improved the form or merely made it busier. Then study a real egg under one lamp and note how its shape differs from a sphere.

lessons.title: Hatching follows form
lessons.subtitle: Make every mark describe a surface.
lessons.idea: Hatching builds tone from repeated lines. Crosshatching adds another direction. Marks that curve around a form can describe its volume as well as its darkness. Begin lightly so additional layers remain a choice.
lessons.observation: The three patches show parallel, crossed, and curved marks. Darker tone comes from closer spacing and additional layers. Curved marks suggest a rounded surface rather than a flat patch.
steps: Fill the first patch with evenly spaced parallel lines.
Add a second direction to the next patch, leaving small gaps of paper.
Use curved hatching to describe a cylinder without filling it with a solid color.
lessons.check: Are my marks describing the surface as well as its value?
lessons.transfer: Draw a folded towel using one hatch direction per plane.

workshop.setup: Choose a comfortable line width and make a few test hatches before the study. Use the fabric reference to find planes and turning surfaces, not to copy every thread.
workshop.demonstration: Begin with three broad tonal areas rather than filling the entire subject with a uniform texture. In the lightest area, leave wide gaps between strokes. In the middle area, bring the strokes closer or add a second layer. In the darkest area, cross the first direction deliberately while keeping the overall plane readable. The direction of the marks should help describe the surface: straighter groups can describe a flatter fold, and curving groups can turn over a rounded ridge. Pause before changing direction so the next layer has a clear purpose. Compare the study at a distance after each pass. If the form already reads, you may need only a small number of extra marks near the focal area. The independent version should test whether hatching can describe volume without relying on a heavy enclosing contour.
workshop.mistakes: A mesh of equally strong lines can obscure the form you meant to explain. Return to broad value groups and choose one principal direction for each plane. If every patch becomes too dark, leave a new area of paper and rebuild more slowly. Avoid drawing random crosshatches just because a section still looks unfinished.
workshop.challenge: Make three small fabric studies: one with parallel hatching, one with crosshatching, and one with marks that change direction with the folds. Limit each to four minutes. Compare which method best explains a particular ridge or valley. Choose one study to develop selectively, adding detail only where it improves the turning form.

lessons.title: A room in perspective
lessons.subtitle: Let parallel edges meet at a distance.
lessons.idea: In one-point perspective, edges that travel straight away from you converge toward one vanishing point on the horizon. Vertical edges remain vertical and edges parallel to the picture plane remain horizontal in this simple setup.
lessons.observation: The room's floor and ceiling edges aim toward the same point. The rectangle at the back is smaller, but its corners sit on the converging lines. The horizon represents the viewer's eye level.
steps: Place the vanishing point and draw a horizontal horizon through it.
Connect the room's outer corners to the vanishing point, then draw the back wall.
Hide the guide and invent a room with a window aligned to the same point.
lessons.check: Do all edges moving away from me aim toward the same point?
lessons.transfer: Look along a hallway and sketch where its ceiling and floor edges appear to meet.

workshop.setup: Use a light construction and leave enough margin to extend perspective lines. Keep your device or paper steady so you can compare the room's main directions.
workshop.demonstration: Find the horizon by comparing the room's receding floor and ceiling edges. In this simple front-facing setup, those directions lead toward one vanishing point. Mark that point lightly and draw a level horizon through it. Place the back wall as a rectangle, then connect its corners toward the nearer edges of your frame. Compare the wall, floor, and ceiling proportions before adding a window. A window on a side wall belongs to that wall's plane, so its receding horizontal edges should follow the same perspective structure. Vertical edges stay vertical in this level view. Keep construction lines long enough to check but lighter than the final visible boundaries. In the final pass, invent a room using the same point and change one feature at a time rather than adding several unrelated perspective systems.
workshop.mistakes: If the room feels twisted, compare the major receding edges before changing details. Do not send front-facing horizontal edges or vertical edges to the vanishing point. A horizon placed too high or low changes the viewpoint, so choose it deliberately. Avoid darkening construction lines that pass through solid walls in the finished study.
workshop.challenge: Draw a simple room from the reference using only its enclosing planes and one window. Then make a second room from imagination with the horizon lower. Compare how much floor and ceiling becomes visible. Finally sketch a real hallway and note where its observed edges meet rather than forcing it to match your invented room.

lessons.title: Build a cylinder
lessons.subtitle: Connect ellipses into a believable object.
lessons.idea: A cylinder combines two circular ends and a continuous side. The ellipses share a center axis. When you see a cylinder below eye level, its lower ellipse often appears more open than the upper one.
lessons.observation: The side edges meet the ellipses smoothly. The back half of the bottom ellipse is construction: it helps establish the form, but a finished opaque cylinder would hide it.
steps: Draw a center axis and place two ellipses along it.
Join their outer edges with straight, parallel sides.
Hide the guide and turn the cylinder into a tin, a candle, or a flowerpot.
lessons.check: Do the ellipses share an axis and connect without pointed corners?
lessons.transfer: Sketch three cylindrical objects at different heights relative to your eyes.

workshop.setup: Use the construction diagram for the basic relationship, then compare it with the tin reference. Begin lightly and keep the center direction visible.
workshop.demonstration: Place the cylinder's top and bottom along a shared axis. Establish the top ellipse's long and short directions, then compare the lower end's apparent openness. Join the outermost sides with smooth tangent transitions, avoiding pointed corners where straight side edges meet the ellipses. The back half of a lower construction ellipse may help you understand the form, but it would be hidden by an opaque object in a finished view. Distinguish that construction from a visible bottom contour. Compare the tin's width with its full height before shading. Then build one broad shadow side and a separate cast shadow, keeping the rim's thickness readable. In the independent pass, transform the same structure into a candle or pot while preserving the shared axis and the way the sides connect to the ends.
workshop.mistakes: Two ellipses with unrelated tilts can make the cylinder look bent. Compare their centers and axes before refining them. If the bottom looks pointed, check the rounded end and side transition. Avoid showing the full hidden bottom ellipse as a dark final line unless the object is transparent and that edge is actually visible.
workshop.challenge: Draw three cylinders: a wide tin, a narrow candle, and a tapered pot. Give each a different height-to-width ratio. Develop only one with light and shadow. Compare the openings with real objects at different eye levels, then note one construction line that should disappear in the finished opaque version.

lessons.title: A botanical study
lessons.subtitle: Grow a complex drawing from one gesture.
lessons.idea: Botanical drawing begins with growth and rhythm. Establish the main stem and the direction of each leaf before its contour. Repetition becomes more convincing when sizes and angles vary naturally.
lessons.observation: Leaves branch from the main stem with different tilts. Each has a central gesture and two edges. The intervals between leaves matter as much as the leaves themselves.
steps: Draw the stem's movement and short directions for each leaf.
Build leaf contours around those directions, varying their widths.
Hide the guide and draw a real sprig, preserving its irregular spacing.
lessons.check: Does every leaf feel connected to the same growing stem?
lessons.transfer: Make two studies of the same plant: one with only gestures and one with contours.

workshop.setup: Begin with the Pencil tool and choose a plant large enough to see its branching. Keep detail secondary until the growth pattern is clear.
workshop.demonstration: Follow the rosemary from its base to its tip and identify the main change of direction. Draw that movement first, then mark where the leaf groups attach. Compare their spacing rather than distributing them evenly. Place a short direction for each group before outlining any individual leaf. The narrow leaves have their own tilts, and some turn partly away from you; compare their apparent widths instead of using one repeated shape. Build only the leaves that explain the branch's rhythm. Once the whole sprig reads, add selective shadows where forms overlap and a few accents near the growing tip. In the independent pass, change the branch's overall gesture and reconstruct a believable new arrangement. Keep the botanical logic of connected growth even when you simplify the individual contours.
workshop.mistakes: A row of identical leaves resembles a decorative pattern more than a growing plant. Vary the size, tilt, and interval according to observation. If leaves appear to float, check their attachment to the stem before adding veins. Avoid making every branch equally dark; choose the main structural route and let smaller growth stay lighter.
workshop.challenge: Make one two-minute gesture study and one ten-minute contour study of the same sprig. Then hide the source and invent a related branch with different spacing. Compare where the independent version loses its sense of growth. Draw a real herb or houseplant afterward and identify a structural difference from the reference.

lessons.title: Catch the gesture
lessons.subtitle: Draw action before anatomy.
lessons.idea: Gesture describes movement, balance, and energy. Begin with the main sweep of the pose, then place the head, rib cage, and pelvis as simple masses. A gesture study can be informative without finished anatomy.
lessons.observation: The curved action line connects the leaning head and torso to the supporting leg. The shoulder and hip tilts differ, giving the pose its rhythm. Avoid treating the limbs as isolated sticks.
steps: Draw the action line in a single sweeping stroke.
Place the head, torso, and pelvis; connect the limbs to those masses.
Hide the guide and invent three poses using no more than ten strokes each.
lessons.check: Can I read the movement before seeing any small features?
lessons.transfer: Draw three quick poses from your own photographs, focusing on balance rather than likeness.

workshop.setup: Use broad, light movements. The mannequin supplies a pose to observe; it is a simplified construction reference rather than a lesson in detailed human anatomy.
workshop.demonstration: Look for the pose's main movement from the head through the torso toward the supporting leg. Draw that action as one sweep before placing the smaller masses. Mark the shoulder and pelvis tilts and compare whether they reinforce or oppose each other. Place the head, rib cage, and pelvis as simple forms along the movement, then connect the limbs. Check where the figure's weight reaches the ground. A pose can lean, but its support still needs to make sense. Keep the first attempt brief enough that you cannot become absorbed in fingers or facial details. In a second pass, change the balance or reach of one limb and see how the rest of the body needs to respond. Gesture records an action relationship, not a collection of unrelated sticks.
workshop.mistakes: If the figure looks rigid, compare the shoulder and hip tilts before adding curves everywhere. If it seems to fall, find the supporting contact and relate it to the body's mass. Do not use the mannequin's mechanical joints as a substitute for studying real anatomy later; they are only a clear starting structure.
workshop.challenge: Draw three one-minute versions of the pose, using no more than ten strokes for each. Choose the clearest and develop the three main body masses. Then make a new balanced action from imagination. Compare it with a photograph you have permission to use and record one difference in the actual body's movement.

lessons.title: Compose with empty space
lessons.subtitle: Decide where the viewer looks first.
lessons.idea: Composition is the arrangement of attention. Size, placement, overlap, and empty space can establish a focal point. Small thumbnails let you compare arrangements before committing to a larger drawing.
lessons.observation: The three little frames rearrange the same circle and rectangle. Compare the quiet centered layout with the off-center version and the version with a smaller focal shape. No layout is automatically best; each creates a different emphasis.
steps: Copy the three thumbnails, keeping their frames the same size.
Make one object dominant through scale or placement in each version.
Hide the guide and create a fourth layout with generous empty space.
lessons.check: Can I name the first place my eye lands in each composition?
lessons.transfer: Arrange two photos in the reference studio and compare three placements before tracing.

workshop.setup: Keep your thumbnails small enough that details are impractical. Use the same rectangular frame for each version so the arrangements are easy to compare.
workshop.demonstration: Start with the orange, cup, and sketchbook as simple flat masses. Decide which should attract attention first, then test a composition through scale, placement, and the amount of empty space around it. In one thumbnail, bring the objects close together; in another, open the interval between them. In a third, crop part of one object at the frame edge while keeping its relationship understandable. Compare where your eye lands in each version. A centered arrangement can feel quiet, while an off-center one may create a different balance; neither is automatically better. Choose the arrangement that supports your intention, not a rule you have heard about an ideal position. Develop only the large value pattern before committing to a longer drawing. Keep the quiet space genuinely quiet so the focal area has something to contrast with.
workshop.mistakes: A focal point is hard to read when every object has the same size and contrast. Change one relationship deliberately rather than adding decorations. If the empty space feels accidental, compare its shape with the group of objects. Avoid using a crop that removes every grounding contact and makes the arrangement appear to float.
workshop.challenge: Make four thumbnails of the same three objects. Change only one variable in each: spacing, scale, crop, or value emphasis. Choose one to develop for ten minutes and explain the choice in your reflection. Revisit the other versions later to see whether a different intention would make one of them more useful.

lessons.title: Trace, fade, remember
lessons.subtitle: Use a reference as a bridge to independence.
lessons.idea: Tracing can make a structure easier to notice, but copying alone does not test what you remember. Use three passes: an attentive trace, a faintly guided reconstruction, and a drawing made with the guide hidden.
lessons.observation: The flower uses a central disk, a ring of petals, and a curved stem. Those are the relationships to remember. You do not need to memorize every irregularity to rebuild its structure.
steps: In Guide mode, trace the flower and say its main parts to yourself.
Switch to Faint. Reconstruct the flower beside your traced version.
Choose Freehand and draw a third flower from memory. Reveal the guide to compare.
lessons.check: Which relationship did I remember, and which would I check next time?
lessons.transfer: Repeat the three-pass method with a reference photo you own. Change its arrangement in the final drawing.

workshop.setup: Plan three separate drawing spaces. Keep the first reference visible, reduce it for the second pass, and hide it for the final reconstruction.
workshop.demonstration: Study the daisy as a small set of relationships: central disk, outer petal spread, stem direction, and leaf attachments. During the first trace, describe those parts to yourself instead of following the edge passively. Pause at a change of direction and notice how the next part connects. For the second pass, use a faint guide and reconstruct the main relationships before refining individual petals. For the third, hide the source and draw from the structure you remember. Reveal the reference only after you have committed to the independent version. Compare the disk's size, the spread of petals, and the stem's route. Choose one relationship to study again; a mismatch is information about your attention, not a verdict on your ability. A final variation can change the flower's tilt while keeping the same basic organization.
workshop.mistakes: An accurate trace can feel successful without leaving you able to reconstruct the subject. Name the structural decisions as you make them. If the memory version loses all proportion, reduce the number of relationships you are trying to remember. Avoid correcting the independent version while the source is already visible; finish it first, then compare.
workshop.challenge: Make the three passes on one page or in three short sessions, spending no more than four minutes on each. Write the most memorable relationship beside the final study. Repeat the method with a photo you own, and change the arrangement in the last pass so the exercise leads toward interpretation rather than permanent dependence on tracing.

lessons.title: Your first personal study
lessons.subtitle: Bring observation, structure, and choice together.
lessons.idea: A personal study combines the skills you have practiced with a choice of your own. Pick a simple subject, decide what interests you, and use only the tools that serve that intention. Finishing means making a clear decision, not adding every detail.
lessons.observation: The still life combines a rounded fruit, a cylindrical cup, and a shared ground. Notice the overlap and the single light direction. You can use this arrangement or substitute objects near you.
steps: Make a tiny composition plan, then block in the large shapes lightly.
Check negative spaces and proportions before adding three clear values.
Hide the guide and make your own variation. Write one observation and one next step in your journal.
lessons.check: Is there one clear focal point, and do my shadows share a light direction?
lessons.transfer: Return to the same objects tomorrow and draw them again from a new viewpoint.

workshop.setup: Choose a reference you want to spend time with, including the desk scene or a photograph you own. Allow enough time for a small plan, a drawing, and a reflection.
workshop.demonstration: Begin by deciding what interests you: the gap around the chair, the vase's silhouette, the window light, or the arrangement as a whole. Write that intention in a few words. Make a small thumbnail and establish the largest shapes before details. Compare the negative spaces and the object's height-to-width relationships. Then choose three clear values and a single main light direction. Keep returning to your intention when deciding where to add detail. The focal area may need a sharper edge or a compact dark accent, while the margins can stay simpler. At the end, view the study at a small size and ask whether the main idea still reads. A personal drawing does not need to reproduce every feature of its source. Its completeness comes from a coherent set of decisions and a useful next step.
workshop.mistakes: When everything seems equally important, return to the original intention and simplify one area. Do not keep adding detail just to postpone deciding that the study is finished. If the arrangement feels wrong, compare the large shape and empty-space relationships before changing tiny marks. A final reflection should identify something visible and specific.
workshop.challenge: Complete a fifteen-minute study and export a copy. Compare it with an early lesson drawing, describing one actual improvement in proportion, edge choice, or value. Return to the same subject the next day from another viewpoint. Keep the first version so the comparison shows what changed through observation and practice.

lessons.title: Stem before leaves
lessons.subtitle: Find the plant's main movement.
lessons.idea: A stem is a route through the drawing. Establish its bends and the attachment points before surrounding it with leaves. A flexible plant rarely follows a ruler-straight axis; its changes of direction organize the whole study.
lessons.observation: Follow the fern from its base to the tip. The small leaves belong to a shared structure rather than floating independently.
steps: Draw the main stem as one slow gesture.
Place only the attachment points and short leaf directions.
Hide the guide and rebuild the branch from its rhythm.
lessons.check: Do the leaves feel connected to one growing structure?
lessons.transfer: Draw the gesture of a real herb sprig before its outline.

workshop.setup: Keep the whole branch visible and begin with a light pencil. Set aside a second area for an independent reconstruction rather than working repeatedly over the first trace.
workshop.demonstration: Find the base of the fern and let your eye travel to its tip. Describe the main route with one line, including any gentle change of direction. Mark only the largest branching points. Compare the intervals between them before placing the smaller leaf groups. Each group has a direction that relates to the stem, but the groups are not identical in length or spacing. Draw those directions as short gestures, then build a few leaf masses around them. Leave some groups unfinished so the underlying organization remains visible. Check the empty wedges between branches; they often reveal when a group has become too wide or too upright. In the final pass, hide the reference and reconstruct the branch from the main stem and attachment rhythm. Reveal it afterward to identify one missed interval. Your goal is a connected growing structure, not a perfect inventory of tiny leaves.
workshop.mistakes: If every branch leaves the stem at the same angle, compare the source's irregularities and vary the next pass deliberately. If the fern looks heavy, check whether too many overlapping lines have replaced the open gaps. Do not repair small leaves before correcting the main stem's direction; the whole group depends on that first relationship.
workshop.challenge: Make a two-minute stem map, a five-minute branch map, and a ten-minute selective contour study. Keep all three so you can see which information each stage contributes. Then draw a real herb sprig using the same sequence, identifying one difference in its attachment pattern and one change you would make in another study.

lessons.title: A leaf inside an envelope
lessons.subtitle: Simplify before describing.
lessons.idea: An envelope is a small set of straight edges that contains a curved form. It gives you a width, height, and tilt to check before the contour becomes complicated. Correct the envelope while it is still light.
lessons.observation: Compare one broad leaf with a narrow one. Their widest points occur at different distances from their tips.
steps: Choose one leaf and mark its tip and base.
Join four straight segments around its outer boundary.
Fade the image and fit a continuous contour inside that boundary.
lessons.check: Did the width and tilt survive the refinement?
lessons.transfer: Block in three leaves from a plant using four lines each.

workshop.setup: Choose the maple leaf's overall silhouette as your subject. Use light straight marks first, leaving the serrated edge and small veins for a later decision.
workshop.demonstration: Mark the stem attachment, the highest tip, and the two widest points. Imagine a simple polygon around the entire leaf, passing outside the smaller indentations. Compare the envelope's width, height, and tilt before you trace any lobe. Next locate the deepest gaps between the main lobes and relate them to the whole boundary. Replace one segment of the envelope with the observed curve, then check whether that refinement changed the total proportion. Repeat around the leaf without letting a small local detail pull the whole shape outward. Once the contour is convincing, add only the main vein directions that explain the lobes. In an independent pass, redraw the envelope at half size and see whether the same asymmetry remains. An envelope is useful because it gives you a few large decisions to compare, not because a plant should become a perfectly regular geometric shape.
workshop.mistakes: Too many segments make an envelope as complicated as the contour it is meant to simplify. Reduce the first pass to five or six directions. If a lobe becomes oversized, check its relationship to the far side of the leaf. Avoid treating the center vein as a demand for symmetry; real leaves often differ on their two sides.
workshop.challenge: Draw the reference leaf twice: once beginning with an envelope and once beginning directly with the contour. Give each the same time. Compare the widest point, overall tilt, and lobe spacing. Finish with a nearby leaf of another kind, using the method that helped you make the clearest large-shape decisions.

lessons.title: The gaps between leaves
lessons.subtitle: Draw the air around a plant.
lessons.idea: Negative shapes have angles and proportions of their own. Comparing those unfamiliar shapes can interrupt the habit of drawing a memorized leaf symbol. A convincing gap often fixes both neighboring leaves at once.
lessons.observation: Look at a triangular opening between two branches and a narrow slit between neighboring leaves.
steps: Outline three empty gaps without drawing leaf veins.
Connect the plant edges that enclose those gaps.
Hide the reference and invent a branch with three different gaps.
lessons.check: Are my gaps varied rather than evenly stamped?
lessons.transfer: Sketch the spaces in a kitchen whisk or a wire basket.

workshop.setup: Use the branch's empty spaces as the starting subject. Begin without veins or shading, and give yourself room to redraw a gap beside the first attempt.
workshop.demonstration: Choose a triangular gap between two leaves and compare its longest direction with its width. Draw that empty shape before describing either leaf. Choose a second gap that is narrower or tilted differently, then locate it in relation to the first. Let the plant boundaries grow around these spaces. The method works because an unfamiliar gap is less likely to trigger a memorized leaf symbol. Keep comparing the total branch width as you work; accurate isolated gaps can still drift apart if their positions are unrelated. Add the stem only where it is visible between the leaves, and allow hidden sections to remain implied. In the final version, simplify the plant to three large gaps and a few connecting contours. Ask whether those empty shapes carry enough information to make the branch feel airy and connected. Then use the same observation strategy on an object whose familiar name usually distracts you from its shape.
workshop.mistakes: Evenly sized gaps create a decorative pattern rather than the source's irregular rhythm. Compare one wide and one narrow opening deliberately. If leaves become disconnected, check the small attachment area at the stem. Avoid filling every gap with dark shading: first establish its actual shape and compare its value with the surrounding background.
workshop.challenge: Make a drawing beginning with three negative spaces and another beginning with the plant's positive shapes. Compare how each method affects leaf spacing. Then draw the holes of a whisk, basket, or chair. Record one proportion you corrected more easily by looking at the air around the object than at the object itself.

lessons.title: Leaves that turn away
lessons.subtitle: Notice the narrowing surface.
lessons.idea: A leaf turning away presents a smaller visible surface. Compare its apparent width with its length instead of assuming that every leaf has the same shape. Its central vein can help you track the turn.
lessons.observation: Some leaves show broad faces while others narrow toward an edge. Compare their visible widths along their central directions.
steps: Choose a broad leaf and a narrower neighboring one.
Draw both central directions and compare their widths.
Reconstruct the pair with a faint guide, keeping their different tilts.
lessons.check: Can I tell which leaf turns away from me?
lessons.transfer: Turn a real leaf in your hand and sketch three viewpoints.

workshop.setup: Keep both leaves visible and compare their apparent widths. Start with central directions and outer landmarks before any vein pattern or surface shading.
workshop.demonstration: Draw a simple line from the base toward the tip of the flatter leaf. Place its widest point across that direction. Now repeat for the turning leaf, comparing how much narrower its visible surface becomes. Do not use the first leaf as a stamp for the second. Look for where a boundary bends, disappears behind another surface, or becomes a thin edge. Mark those turning points lightly and connect them with a restrained contour. The central vein is a helpful path through the form, but it may not sit exactly halfway between the visible boundaries when the leaf turns. Add a small amount of shading only after the two silhouettes show different orientations. For the independent study, invent another turn of the same kind of leaf and check it against a real leaf or folded piece of paper. Predict the change in width, then observe rather than insisting on the prediction.
workshop.mistakes: A turning leaf can look like a smaller front-facing leaf if you shrink both dimensions equally. Compare which dimension actually compresses. Avoid making the central vein a straight symmetrical divider. If the leaf feels folded like cardboard, soften the transition and compare the broad curved surface before adding a sharp crease.
workshop.challenge: Make three small studies of one real leaf as you turn it toward and away from your eyes. Keep its length approximately consistent on the page and compare the changing width and visible edge. Beside the studies, write which landmark stayed useful throughout the turn and which boundary changed most.

lessons.title: Hatching a green surface
lessons.subtitle: Turn color into value.
lessons.idea: Green does not have to become a single dark patch. Look for the light and shadow within each leaf, then choose a small group of values. Curved hatches can describe the surface without outlining every vein.
lessons.observation: Compare the lit leaf edges with darker overlaps. Small veins are less important than the broad light pattern.
steps: Draw one leaf lightly and leave its brightest strip empty.
Curve a few hatches from the central vein toward the edge.
Hide the guide and describe a second leaf using only three values.
lessons.check: Do the hatches help the leaf turn in space?
lessons.transfer: Draw a real leaf in monochrome under one lamp.

workshop.setup: Use the Monochrome view to check value when needed, then return to color for observation. Keep your first hatches light enough to add another layer deliberately.
workshop.demonstration: Outline the fig leaf's broad shape and place the central vein. Squint at the reference to separate the largest light and shadow areas before thinking about the color green. Reserve the brightest area as paper, and build a middle value with spaced curved strokes that turn away from the central structure. In a darker fold or overlap, add a second group rather than pressing heavily over the entire leaf. Compare whether the marks describe the changing surface as well as its lightness. Small veins need only a few selected accents; they should not become an equally dark net over the drawing. Pause and view the study at a small size. If the leaf's form still reads, add detail only near one focal area. In the independent pass, choose another leaf and adapt the hatch directions to its different surface instead of repeating the same pattern.
workshop.mistakes: A uniform green-to-gray fill ignores the light falling on the leaf. Compare lit and shadowed regions within the same local color. If every vein is dark, the surface can look etched rather than flexible. Reduce the vein emphasis and return to broad hatching. Avoid hatching in one direction across a surface that visibly turns.
workshop.challenge: Draw one leaf with three values and no interior vein lines, then another with selective veins added after the value plan. Compare which marks actually explain the surface. For a final ten-minute study, use a real leaf under one lamp and choose hatch directions before making the first tonal patch.

lessons.title: A flower seen at an angle
lessons.subtitle: Build the disk before the petals.
lessons.idea: A flower head can be organized around a tilted disk. The visible disk becomes narrower as it turns away, while the petals overlap around it. This is a starting structure, not a rule that every flower is perfectly circular.
lessons.observation: Compare the forward-facing cosmos with a flower tilted sideways. Their centers and petal spreads have different proportions.
steps: Mark the center and tilt of each flower head.
Sketch a light ellipse around each spread of petals.
Fade the guide and place the petals around those ellipses.
lessons.check: Do the heads face different directions?
lessons.transfer: Draw the same simple flower from above and from the side.

workshop.setup: Keep the complete flower arrangement visible for the first pass. Draw lightly and leave separate room for the different flower-head orientations.
workshop.demonstration: Begin with the center of each flower head and a short line indicating its tilt. Imagine an ellipse around the broad petal spread, comparing the forward-facing head with the narrower side view. Draw those envelopes before separating individual petals. Their purpose is to establish orientation, not to force every irregular petal tip onto a perfect oval. Place the central disk inside each envelope and compare how much of it is visible. Add the larger front petals first, then allow rear petals to stop at overlaps. Relate each head to its stem so the flowers belong to the same arrangement. In a second pass, keep only the envelopes, disks, and stem gestures. If those few marks show three different directions, the structural study has worked. Hide the guide for the final reconstruction, then compare the apparent openness of the heads when you reveal it again.
workshop.mistakes: Drawing every head as the same circle makes the bouquet look pressed flat. Compare the side-facing flower's width-to-height relationship before adding petals. If the disk sits in the wrong place, check the entire envelope rather than shifting petals individually. Avoid sharpening natural petals into identical points; their outer rhythm should stay irregular.
workshop.challenge: Make a small orientation study of all three heads using only ellipses, disks, and stems. Choose one to develop with overlapping petals. Then draw the same simple flower from two imagined viewpoints and compare the changes with a real flower or a permitted photograph. Note one direction you find difficult to remember.

lessons.title: Petals in front and behind
lessons.subtitle: Let overlap explain depth.
lessons.idea: Overlapping petals create small T-shaped junctions: one edge stops where another passes in front. Draw the front edge continuously and allow the hidden edge to stop. A dark outline around every petal can flatten the flower.
lessons.observation: Find a petal that covers its neighbor. Notice the edge that continues and the edge that disappears.
steps: Choose three overlapping petals and draw the nearest first.
Stop the rear contours where they become hidden.
Hide the guide and invent a small cluster with the same overlap order.
lessons.check: Can I name which petal is nearest without shading?
lessons.transfer: Arrange three paper scraps and sketch their overlaps.

workshop.setup: Use the peony as a study of overlap rather than an assignment to count every petal. Begin with a large flower envelope and choose a small focal cluster.
workshop.demonstration: Locate the flower's outer spread and broad center before drawing internal boundaries. Find one petal that clearly passes in front of another. Draw its continuing edge and stop the rear edge where it becomes hidden. Add a third petal using the same front-to-back logic. These small junctions are more useful than an uninterrupted dark outline around every petal. Compare the cluster's light and shadow shapes after the overlap reads. A soft petal can turn gradually into shadow, while a folded lip may make a sharper edge; use the reference to choose. Keep the rest of the flower simpler so the focal cluster has contrast. In the independent pass, invent a new three-petal group while preserving a believable overlap order. The aim is to understand depth through interruption, not to reproduce the reference's exact number of petals.
workshop.mistakes: A petal becomes a flat sticker when every boundary receives the same heavy line. Choose which edge is in front and let the hidden edge stop. If the cluster looks tangled, remove one unnecessary contour and compare the junction again. Do not use shading to conceal an uncertain overlap; resolve the edge order first.
workshop.challenge: Draw three overlapping petals with no shading, then add two values to clarify the turning surfaces. Make a second cluster from imagination and label the front-to-back order in your reflection. Transfer the exercise to three paper scraps, checking whether the same contour interruptions explain their very different material.

lessons.title: Stems through a glass
lessons.subtitle: Separate what you see from what you expect.
lessons.idea: Transparent objects mix visible contours, reflections, and displaced views of what lies behind them. Draw the shapes actually visible through the glass. Avoid forcing the stems into perfectly continuous lines when the image shows an offset.
lessons.observation: The glass rim, water boundary, and stems make several distinct edges. Keep them separate rather than drawing one heavy cylinder.
steps: Lightly establish the outer glass and its rim.
Locate only the visible stem segments inside it.
Add two or three reflected light shapes, leaving most glass unshaded.
lessons.check: Does the glass feel transparent rather than metallic?
lessons.transfer: Observe a spoon in a real glass of water without assuming its shape.

workshop.setup: Start with the whole glass and flower stems in view. Use light marks and distinguish the outer vessel, water boundary, and visible stem segments as separate observations.
workshop.demonstration: Establish the glass's width, height, and rim before drawing the stems inside it. Locate where the water meets the vessel and compare that boundary with the rim's ellipse. Follow one stem above the water, then look carefully at the segment visible through the glass rather than assuming it continues in a straight line. The combined effects of water, glass curvature, and viewpoint can displace or distort its visible shape. Draw the observed segment and leave the uncertain section simple. Add only a few selected reflection boundaries to suggest the glass surface; most of the vessel can remain unshaded. Check whether the stems still feel connected to the flowers even where their visible routes change. In the final pass, use fewer internal marks and compare whether transparency becomes clearer. A transparent object is described by relationships across its surface, not by filling it with a generic gray tone.
workshop.mistakes: A rigid uninterrupted stem can contradict the actual view through water. Check each visible segment independently before connecting it. If the glass looks metallic, reduce broad dark fills and reserve reflected light shapes. Avoid outlining every reflection equally; compare which boundaries are compact and which fade into the surrounding value.
workshop.challenge: Make one study of the glass and two stem routes without flowers, then a second including the whole arrangement. Compare the rim, waterline, and stem offsets. Observe a real spoon or stem in a glass of water afterward, noting which change belongs to the observed view rather than to your prior idea of the object.

lessons.title: A bouquet in three values
lessons.subtitle: Group the light before the detail.
lessons.idea: A tonal plan reduces a complex subject to a few large families. White petals can remain mostly paper while dark background gaps describe their edges. Preserve the shared light pattern before selecting any petal veins.
lessons.observation: Squint at the flowers, glass, and background. Separate the brightest petals, middle stems, and darker spaces.
steps: Make three small value swatches beside your study.
Block the bouquet as large connected light and dark shapes.
Fade the guide and add detail to only one flower head.
lessons.check: Does the bouquet still read when viewed small?
lessons.transfer: Photograph a bouquet you own and simplify it to three values.

workshop.setup: Use a small thumbnail before the larger study and keep the Monochrome reference option available. Limit the initial plan to three clearly separated value families.
workshop.demonstration: Squint at the anemones and identify the largest bright mass, the middle-value structure, and the darkest surrounding spaces. Sketch those groups without drawing each petal. Where neighboring light petals merge, allow them to remain one shape until a boundary is needed to explain overlap. Keep the vase related to the bouquet's overall dark pattern instead of treating it as a separate rendering exercise. After the three-value thumbnail reads, enlarge the arrangement and add one selected flower head in greater detail. Its petal turns can include a few intermediate tones, but they should remain subordinate to the original broad grouping. Compare the drawing at a distance after each refinement. If the bouquet becomes less readable as detail increases, return to the large masses. In an independent version, change the crop while preserving the same light-to-dark organization.
workshop.mistakes: A separate outline around every white petal can destroy the shared light mass. Let value differences describe only the important separations. If the middle tones multiply until everything looks gray, choose a smaller set again. Do not add bright highlights everywhere; preserve the contrast that made the initial thumbnail clear.
workshop.challenge: Create three tiny versions of the bouquet using three values, changing the crop each time. Choose one for a fifteen-minute study and develop only a single flower head. In your reflection, describe which small detail improved the large value design and which mark you could remove without losing useful information.

lessons.title: A botanical page of your own
lessons.subtitle: Combine structure and selective detail.
lessons.idea: A study page can explain how a plant works without rendering every part equally. Combine an overall gesture, one enlarged detail, and a small memory drawing. Changing scale makes the page more informative than a single laborious copy.
lessons.observation: Compare the fern's repeated growth with the cosmos arrangement. Choose the plant whose structure interests you most.
steps: Draw one small whole-plant study from the reference.
Enlarge one leaf or petal and describe its turning surface.
Hide the guide and make a memory sketch; write what changed.
lessons.check: Does each drawing on my page have a different purpose?
lessons.transfer: Make the same three-part page from a plant near your home.

workshop.setup: Treat the basil plant as a subject for a complete study page. Reserve room for a whole-plant view, one enlarged detail, and a small independent reconstruction.
workshop.demonstration: Find the plant's main stem directions and the overall reach of its leaves before drawing the pot. Place a light envelope around the whole plant, then compare the branching within it. Build a small whole-plant study that emphasizes attachment and spacing rather than every vein. Next choose one leaf whose turn interests you. Enlarge that detail beside the first study and describe its contour, central direction, and broad light pattern. The change of scale lets you study information that would become clutter in the small drawing. For the last view, hide the reference and reconstruct the plant's main growth pattern in a few marks. Reveal the source afterward and compare one branch junction. The page should show three kinds of observation, not three increasingly elaborate copies. Finish with a short note that connects the detail study back to the structure of the whole plant.
workshop.mistakes: If the enlarged detail overwhelms the page, make a small layout plan before continuing. A whole-plant study becomes confusing when every leaf is equally finished. Choose a few that explain the growth and let the others stay simple. Avoid judging the memory sketch by detail count; compare its main branching relationships instead.
workshop.challenge: Create the three-part botanical page from the reference, then repeat it from a real plant on another day. Keep the overall study small, develop one turning leaf, and add a memory map. Compare the two pages in My practice and identify one observation you made from life that the reference did not explain clearly.

lessons.title: Two pears, two silhouettes
lessons.subtitle: Look past the label of the object.
lessons.idea: Two objects with the same name can have very different boundaries. Compare the shoulder width, lean, and low bulge of each pear. An irregular silhouette usually carries more character than decorative spots.
lessons.observation: One pear stands while the other rests at a different angle. Their stems do not point in the same direction.
steps: Mark each pear's top, bottom, and widest points.
Connect those landmarks with a light angular envelope.
Fade the guide and refine only the contours that change direction.
lessons.check: Can I distinguish the two pears by outline alone?
lessons.transfer: Draw two real pieces of fruit without any interior marks.

workshop.setup: Begin with the two pears as separate silhouettes and leave texture until the end. Use a light pencil so you can compare and revise their large shapes.
workshop.demonstration: Mark each pear's top, base, widest point, and stem direction. The standing pear and resting pear have different orientations, so compare them independently before relating their positions. Connect the landmarks with a few straight segments, then refine the shoulder and broad lower mass. Look at the gap between the pears and the cup: its shape can reveal a width or placement error. When both silhouettes are convincing, add the simplest shadow family and grounding contact. Small skin spots are optional; they should not distract from the asymmetry that makes the fruit recognizable. Make a second small version using only the two outlines. If their individual character remains visible, you have kept the essential information. For the independent pass, choose two real pieces of fruit and compare their different envelopes rather than drawing two versions of the same memorized pear symbol.
workshop.mistakes: Identical shoulders and bases make two different pears look stamped. Compare their actual lean and widest points. If a stem appears to point in an unrelated direction, connect it back to the fruit's main axis. Do not decorate an incorrect contour with spots; correct the envelope while the drawing is still simple.
workshop.challenge: Draw the pair with no interior marks, then add three values to one pear only. Make another pair from life and compare how little detail each silhouette needs.
