In a second study, omit color information entirely and use only the revised value plan. Compare whether the scene's arrangement and depth remain readable. The exercise develops judgment about lightness rather than a fixed conversion rule for named colors.
workshop.mistakes: Assuming every saturated color is dark can distort the plan. Compare actual grayscale relationships. Outlining a low-contrast boundary may rescue it locally but change the intended emphasis, so decide deliberately. If pots look flat, restore their light and shadow within the local value instead of assigning each object one uniform gray.
workshop.challenge: Make a prediction thumbnail, a checked monochrome plan, and one fifteen-minute drawing. Compare the first two and describe a specific surprise. Use a personal colorful reference for another study, identifying two different colors with similar values and one object whose light and shadow span a wide value range.

lessons.title: Two wheels, one viewpoint
lessons.subtitle: Align the bicycle's large circles.
lessons.idea: A bicycle starts with two wheels and their shared contact with the ground. Depending on the camera angle, the wheels may appear as ellipses. Compare their centers, apparent sizes, and tilt before drawing spokes.
lessons.observation: Look at the two wheels and the line between their contact points. Treat them as observed shapes rather than automatic perfect circles.
steps: Mark the wheel centers and ground contacts.
Draw the two outer wheel shapes with light strokes.
Fade the image and check the wheelbase against wheel height.
lessons.check: Do both wheels belong to one viewpoint and ground plane?
lessons.transfer: Sketch a parked bicycle from your own photograph.

workshop.setup: Begin with the bicycle's two wheels and their ground contacts. Leave spokes, cables, and basket weave out of the first construction, keeping the full machine visible.
workshop.demonstration: Place the centers of both wheels and compare the distance between them with a wheel's apparent diameter. Draw each observed outer shape lightly. Depending on the view, a wheel may appear elliptical, so compare its width and height rather than insisting on a perfect circle. Locate the two ground contacts and the bicycle's lean against its support. Connect the centers through the main frame directions, checking that the fork reaches the front axle and the rear structure meets the back axle. Add the saddle and handlebar masses only after the wheel relationship agrees. Use a few broad values to separate tires, frame, and wall. In a second construction, omit spokes entirely and check whether the bicycle remains coherent. Mechanical details in generated images can be ambiguous; compare unclear joints with a real bicycle or suitable photograph before treating them as precise engineering information.
workshop.mistakes: Accurate spokes cannot rescue wheels placed too close together. Compare centers and diameters first. If the bicycle seems to hover, check both ground contacts and its support. Avoid forcing both wheels into identical page shapes when the actual viewpoint changes their visible size or angle.
workshop.challenge: Draw three bicycle constructions using wheels, centers, frame directions, and ground contacts only. Develop one with selected dark accents. Study a real bicycle or personal photograph for another sketch, recording one proportion or connection that you corrected through observation before adding small mechanical details.

lessons.title: A frame made of angles
lessons.subtitle: Build the structure before components.
lessons.idea: A bicycle frame can be simplified into a few connected segments and triangular gaps. Compare those angles before adding handlebars, chain, or cables. Correcting one triangle can bring several connected parts into alignment.
lessons.observation: Study the main frame triangle and the fork direction. Look at the empty spaces they enclose.
steps: Draw the largest frame triangle between the wheel centers.
Add the fork and seat direction using observed angles.
Hide the guide and rebuild the same frame with fewer lines.
lessons.check: Are the triangular gaps proportionate?
lessons.transfer: Block in the frame of a chair using straight segments.

workshop.setup: Use the blue bicycle's frame and triangular gaps as the main subject. Establish the wheels first and keep the lines light enough to adjust connected angles together.
workshop.demonstration: Mark wheel centers and their apparent sizes. Locate the crank, saddle junction, and upper steering connection as major landmarks. Join them with simple frame directions, comparing the triangular empty spaces rather than treating the bicycle as a list of tubes. Check the fork's route to the front axle and the rear frame's connection to its wheel. If one landmark moves, reconsider the segments that meet it instead of bending a single tube to compensate. Add a suggestion of thickness only after the central structure agrees. Keep cables and chain detail secondary. In a second study, draw the triangular gaps first and build the frame around them. Compare whether that approach improves the angles. Verify ambiguous mechanical connections against a real bicycle or a reliable photograph, because the generated reference is intended for drawing practice rather than engineering accuracy.
workshop.mistakes: Parallel or disconnected tubes can make the frame structurally confusing. Return to shared landmarks and enclosed gaps. If the crank seems misplaced, compare its position with both axles before moving it. Avoid adding decorative hardware to hide a connection you have not understood; simplify and verify the joint first.
workshop.challenge: Make one landmark-and-segment construction and another beginning with the frame's negative triangles. Develop the clearer version with a few thickness and value accents. Draw a chair, bicycle, or other angular object from your own reference, comparing how connected landmarks make several proportions easier to revise together.

lessons.title: Spokes behind the frame
lessons.subtitle: Choose what overlaps and what disappears.
lessons.idea: Complex mechanical subjects become clearer when you establish the overlap order. The frame passes in front of some wheel details, while nearer parts cover farther ones. You do not need every spoke to make a wheel readable.
lessons.observation: Find places where the frame interrupts the wheels. Compare visible and hidden portions of the far side.
steps: Draw the main wheel and frame silhouettes.
Add only a few spokes that explain each wheel's center.
Fade the image and stop hidden lines at the correct overlaps.
lessons.check: Can I explain the front-to-back order of the parts?
lessons.transfer: Draw a wire object while omitting all hidden segments.

workshop.setup: Study the front wheel, fork, and handlebar as overlapping layers. Begin with the wheel envelope and axle before selecting a limited number of spokes to draw.
workshop.demonstration: Place the wheel's outer shape and center, then the tire and rim as related boundaries. Draw the fork in front of the wheel where the viewpoint shows it overlapping. Establish the frame and handlebar connections as larger structural masses. Choose a few spoke directions and let them stop behind the nearer fork or other solid parts. Compare visible near and far elements without drawing every hidden segment through the structure. Add restrained value differences to separate tire, metal, and wall. Keep the brightest reflections selective rather than outlining every shiny surface. In a second study, halve the number of spokes while preserving the overlap order. Check whether the wheel still reads clearly. Use a real bicycle or suitable photograph to verify uncertain connections, since a generated image may simplify small mechanical details inconsistently.
workshop.mistakes: Drawing all spokes through the fork makes the bicycle look transparent. Stop hidden marks at the nearer solid. If the rim becomes uneven, compare its relationship to the outer tire before adding spokes. Avoid assuming more mechanical detail means more accuracy; clear large connections and believable overlaps matter first.
workshop.challenge: Make an overlap diagram with wheel, fork, and three selected spoke groups, then a fifteen-minute value study. Draw a real wheel, fan guard, or layered household object from observation, identifying the nearest element and deliberately omitting the portions it hides. Record how fewer marks can clarify the construction.

lessons.title: Tell a story with a crop
lessons.subtitle: Let the frame make a choice.
lessons.idea: A crop can emphasize the bicycle as an object or the place around it. Compare a close mechanical study with a wider environmental view. Keep essential support and contact information even when parts leave the frame.
lessons.observation: Consider the bicycle's relationship to the wall and paving. Decide whether the subject is the machine or the quiet place.
steps: Draw one close crop and one wider thumbnail.
Choose the version that supports your intended story.
Switch to Freehand and develop only its important shapes and values.
lessons.check: Does the crop communicate the subject I chose?
lessons.transfer: Photograph a personal object in its usual setting and test two crops.

workshop.setup: Plan two crops of the cream bicycle beside the green doorway. Decide whether the subject is the machine itself or the quiet place around it before developing detail.
workshop.demonstration: In the first thumbnail, crop closely around wheels, frame, and basket. Keep enough ground contact to explain the bicycle's support. In the second, include more doorway, wall, and paving so the machine becomes part of an architectural setting. Compare the large light and dark masses in both. Choose the version that supports your intended story and enlarge its main proportions. Establish the wall and ground before detailing spokes or basket weave. Use the bicycle's silhouette and a few characteristic accents to make it readable at the chosen scale. Let less important surfaces remain simple. At the end, compare the study with its thumbnail and remove one accent that distracts from the subject you selected. Verify any unclear mechanical connection through a real object reference rather than enlarging a questionable generated detail.
workshop.mistakes: A crop can become awkward when it removes all support information or cuts exactly through an important joint. Compare a slightly wider and narrower version before committing. If basket texture dominates a scene about place, reduce it. Avoid making every paving stone as prominent as the bicycle's main silhouette.
workshop.challenge: Create two crop thumbnails and one twenty-minute study with a stated story. Explain why the selected frame supports that story. Use a personal object in its surroundings for another pair of crops, comparing an object portrait with an environmental view while preserving believable support and contact in both.

lessons.title: A small portfolio, a next step
lessons.subtitle: Look back and choose deliberately.
lessons.idea: Progress becomes visible through comparison. Revisit an early study and a recent one, describe a specific change, and choose a practical next exercise. A portfolio is a considered selection, not a requirement that every drawing be finished.
lessons.observation: Use the reference as a starting point for a personal final study. Combine your own crop with the skills you now find useful.
steps: Draw one final study of this scene or a personal reference photo.
Compare it with an early saved drawing in My practice.
Write one observed improvement and one precise goal for your next week.
lessons.check: Can I name a visible change instead of judging the whole drawing?
lessons.transfer: Select three exported studies and plan a new subject to draw from life.

workshop.setup: Use the pear, white vase, branch, and sketchbook as a final reference, then choose personal objects for an independent study. Gather one early drawing and one recent drawing for comparison.
workshop.demonstration: Begin by naming a clear intention for the final still life, such as quiet light or contrasting forms. Make two thumbnails that place the pear, vase, and dark sketchbook differently within the frame. Choose one and establish the large envelopes, shared ground, and empty gaps. Compare proportions using a single measuring unit. Build three broad values before selecting details on the branch or book. Vary edges according to light and overlap, leaving some areas economical. Develop one focal relationship and stop when the drawing communicates the intention. Now place it beside an early study from your journal. Describe a specific change in proportion, line confidence, value grouping, or composition, using visible evidence rather than a general judgment of talent. Choose one relationship that still feels uncertain and design a small next exercise for it. Finally repeat the process with personal objects or your own reference photo, making the final choice of crop and emphasis yourself.
workshop.mistakes: A final study does not need every skill or every object in the course. Select the relationships that support the intention. Comparing only polish can hide structural progress, so look at measurable decisions. Avoid treating a difficult drawing as proof of failure; name the particular relationship that needs another observation and plan one manageable exercise.
workshop.challenge: Create a small portfolio of three studies: an early exercise, a recent workshop, and this independent final drawing. Give each a short note about intention, one successful decision, and one next step. Save the final study in My practice and choose a specific lesson to revisit with a new personal reference.
